cells.tense: Present — you're here, deciding, and it's working.
cells.verb: letting go of what's finished so something new has room to grow
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before you can say why
cells.ask: Let that same clean sense of what's done and what's still alive decide one thing between you and another person — what's owed, what's fair, what gets handed back — without working it out on paper first; what comes back is an exchange that evens itself out while you're not watching.
cells.core: You know what to let go of and what to keep, and you know it before you could argue for it. Things that have run their course get cleared without drama, things still growing get tended, and your attention goes to the right one without a committee meeting. That's not luck; it's a sense you've earned and are actually using.\n\nThere's room for it to reach a little further. The knack you have for telling finished from living is the same knack that tells fair from unfair — and it works just as well on what passes between you and other people as on what you're clearing out alone.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's finished and what's still growing, and you don't have to prove it.

cells.tense: Future — you're already living in the ending before it's come.
cells.verb: clearing things out before they're actually finished
cells.place: in the part of you that's supposed to notice what matters now, but is scanning for what's about to be gone
cells.ask: Pick one thing — a plan, a habit, a person's place in your week — that you've half-decided is over, and stay with it for a little while without deciding anything about its fate; let it be exactly as alive as it is, and you alongside it, neither of you swallowing the other. What comes back is endings arriving when they're actually due, and a renewal you don't have to force because it was coming anyway.
cells.core: You're cutting things loose ahead of their time. Somewhere out there is a version of events where it all needed clearing, and you're already there, pruning for it — so your attention lands on what's about to go, not on what's here. Things that were still growing get treated as compost.\n\nThe sense of what to keep and what to release is real in you; it's just running early. The cure isn't to stop knowing. It's to be in the room with what's still alive long enough to find out whether it is.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things before they've finished.

cells.tense: Past — you're still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: holding on to what's finished instead of clearing it
cells.place: in the part of you that should be noticing what matters now, but is still turned toward what was
cells.ask: Don't make yourself let go of anything. Instead, find one thing you actually want to grow — not ought to, want to — and put your effort there for a week, the way you'd water one bed and not the whole garden; the wanting does the clearing for you. What comes back is endings that honor themselves because something new is pulling, and a renewal you can trust because you felt it before you reasoned it.
cells.core: Something's done and you haven't cleared it. Behind you is a room where letting go cost more than it should have, and the sense that knows what's finished has gone quiet rather than risk that again. So the old things stay, and your attention stays with them, and the ground that could be growing something is still full of last season.\n\nThe knowing hasn't left. It's just not being fed — and you can't feed it by forcing the clearing.
cells.sheetLine: You know it's finished. You haven't cleared the ground.

cells.tense: Disowned present — pen down in a room you're already writing.
cells.verb: already deciding what ends, what stays, and what gets your attention
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before you can say why — and you're calling it coincidence
cells.ask: About one thing you've been describing as 'it just ran its course,' say the plainer sentence instead: 'I ended that.' Draw the line out loud, once, where someone can hear it. What comes back is a clarity people can lean on — things make sense around you because the decision is visible, and the endings start to feel chosen instead of suffered.
cells.core: You're already doing it. Things end around you and new things get room, and the order is nearly always right — but you'd describe it as how things happened to go. The choosing is running; the ownership isn't.\n\nThat matters, because a decision nobody claims can't be relied on, including by you. Knowing what's finished is a kind of authority, and it's yours.
cells.sheetLine: You're already choosing what ends. You just call it 'how it went.'
